title: Eighty-eight temples
hook: the Shikoku pilgrimage around Kukai's island, walked by pilgrims in white

segments.voice: Yesterday's pilgrimage climbed Vulture Peak, a ledge at dawn and a flower held up in silence. Your line was the hill of sutras. Did you take the stairs slowly? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-seven.

On a country road in Japan, an old woman steps out of her house and holds out an orange to a stranger. The stranger is dressed all in white, with a wide sedge hat and a wooden staff, and a little bell that rings with each step. The stranger bows, takes the orange, and walks on. The woman goes back inside. Neither of them thinks this is odd. On this island, people in white have been walking past front doors like hers for a very long time, on a road that goes all the way around and comes back to where it started. The island is Shikoku. The road links its temples, and its name is today's word: eighty-eight temples.
screen: `AN ORANGE ON A COUNTRY ROAD.` → `A PILGRIM IN WHITE.` → `A ROAD THAT COMES BACK AROUND.`

segments.voice: First, the teacher behind the road. Kukai, also known as Kobo Daishi, is the teacher tradition credits with bringing the esoteric teaching called Shingon to Japan, and Shikoku is the island tradition calls his home. The pilgrimage follows temples linked with him, in a great loop around the island. The pilgrim is called a henro. Second, the clothes. The white jacket is the mark of a pilgrim. Some say white was chosen because it is the color of burial clothes, so a pilgrim sets out ready for anything the road brings. The staff, tradition says, stands for Kukai himself. Third, two on the road. Some pilgrims' hats carry words that mean two traveling together. The pilgrim may walk alone, but the teaching says Kukai walks beside them the whole way. So at night, tradition says, pilgrims wash the tip of the staff before they wash their own feet: they take care of their companion first. And at each temple, a pilgrim chants, leaves a slip with their name, and has a book stamped with a red seal and brushed with ink. Fourth, the people along the way. Islanders offer pilgrims small gifts, an orange, tea, a ride, a bed. It is called osettai, and the pilgrim receives it as given to Kukai, not to themselves. Some walk the whole loop at once. Others come back a section at a time, over years. Some go by bus or car. However they go, the road brings them back to the temple where they began. A circle, not a line.
screen: `KUKAI'S ISLAND.` · `WHITE CLOTHES, A STAFF, A HAT.` · `TWO TRAVELING TOGETHER.` · then, large: `A CIRCLE, NOT A LINE.`

segments.voice: Here is a small loop of your own, if you'd like and your space allows. Stand, and choose a little circle: around a room, a table, a yard, a block. Walk it slowly. With each step, let the breath be easy. As you walk, remember the two traveling together: whatever or whoever you hold dear, let it walk beside you. When you come back to where you started, stop and bow, or simply stand still. If walking isn't possible, trace a slow circle with your hand. Then sit. The bell holds the time.
Eighty-eight temples. The pilgrimage around Shikoku, Kukai's island, walked by pilgrims in white who, tradition says, never walk alone. Today's word.
Your line: eighty-eight temples. Today, receive one small kindness the way a pilgrim does: with a bow, and passing the thanks along. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Pilgrims on Shikoku, often dressed in white with a hat and staff, visit the temples of the circuit on foot, by bus or by car, chanting at each one and collecting a red seal in a pilgrim's book, while islanders offer them small gifts called osettai.
